title: One foot square of rain on stone: splash, puddles, ripples
notes: A test bench, before going back to the sculpture: heavy rain (100 mm/h) falls for two minutes on a one foot square in the middle of an 8 ft slab of limestone-like stone, nothing else in the scene. Real speed. Seen from 1, 3, 6 and 9 ft away, looking down at 45 degrees. No motion blur, no depth of field: every frame is an instant, drops at their real size.

What happens, and why. The square darkens within seconds: the stone drinks the first rain. Every drop throws a burst of tiny droplets (0.1 to 0.5 mm) that land up to 30-40 cm away, so a soft dark halo of splash grows around the square and fades out with distance. After about 20 seconds the stone's surface is full and water starts to stand; puddles join up and, once they meet stone that splash and wicking have already wetted, they spill past the square in rounded lobes (by 2:00, about 660 cm2 of standing water outside the square). Water also creeps sideways inside the stone, slowly: a few millimetres in two minutes, about 3 cm in an hour.

On the standing water: rings travel out from each impact, cross, bounce off the puddle edges and fade. They are real height, a tenth of a millimetre, so they read faintly. The small clear circles are falling drops; the brief vertical streaks under some of them are their reflections, stretched by the ripples (the way moonlight stretches on rippled water).

Physics, briefly: absorption by sorptivity (S = 0.5 mm/min^0.5, a limestone value), puddle edges held by surface tension on dry stone (about 2.2 mm high) and feathering onto wet stone, splash counts, sizes, speeds and angles from published drop-impact studies, a water balance that accounts for every drop. The code was audited by AI reviewers (three agents and a second model) before this render, and every finding was fixed.
Known limits: no evaporation yet (damp stone never dries); the stone has no colour texture, so the look is plain; ripples in deep water fade a little slower than they should.

title: Where the rain goes: a map of the sky above the sculpture
notes: Which rain ends up inside? To answer it once and for all, a grid of 650,000 particles (one every centimetre, three per square, over the whole site) was dropped from above the sculpture. Each falls, runs downhill along the stone wherever it lands, drips off overhangs, spills over ledges, and is followed until it reaches the ground.

Every square of sky is then coloured by where its water ends up. In still air, rain falling on about 14.4 square metres of sky ends up on the 9 square metres of floor inside. Only 0.4 square metres of it falls straight through the openings without touching stone: most finds its way in by running down the inner walls, along the tubes that reach far out from the building, and through the low openings at the floor. A little more (0.8 square metres) lands on the floor outside and then runs or spills in across it, filling low spots on the way like real puddles.

In a light wind (2 m/s) the rain slants. The openings are tall, narrow shafts, so slanted rain hits their walls instead of falling through: the straight-through share drops to 0.14 square metres, while the water that runs in along the stone stays about the same.
This map now decides where rain is simulated in detail for the views from inside.
